commitments.text: Provide, prior to construction and surface disturbance, a dust mitigation plan acceptable to MEM and MELP. This plan should include measures to effectively minimize and control dust to the extent practical from tailings, mine roads, coal piles, waste dumps and to ensure that MELP Ambient Air Guidelines are met. Further consideration should also be given to modifications to the material storage and handling plans associated with raw and clean coal and tailings as presented in the project report, such as minimizing coal storage and handling at the plant site. In the event that Ambient Air Guidelines are approached at designated monitoring locations off the mine site, an evaluation and assessment of cause and mitigation may be required by MELP.

Surface amendments or other appropriate measures to control dusting from tailings ponds will be used when required. These mitigations could include inundation, surface sprays and a windbreak/dust barrier along the berm.
Dust control program for road surfaces to include incorporation of effective control measures successfully used in BC.

Install dust control systems, acceptable to MEM and MELP, on any coal transfer facilities (truck unloading and rail car loading) and at breaker stations which are dust sources and at any processing operations generating dust which could include dust suppression and treatment.
If determined to be beneficial, construction and vegetation of a berm along the clean coal storage area to improve noise dissipation, to be constructed prior to plant operation.
For blasting, establish limits to the peak particle velocity relative to acceptable standards required to be observed at the nearest residence when mine is operational.
Investigate alternatives to the audible alarms as currently required by the Health, Safety and Reclamation Code for Mines in British Columbia.
If required, follow-up on the Visual Quality Impact Assessment, in co-operation with MEM and MOF (with respect to the Forestry Practices Code).

In discussion with MOTH, attempt to develop an interim management program, which includes provision for a highway lookout point with signs illustrating proposed reclamation plans and providing examples of reclamation for viewing as the project progresses.

Control sediment release from areas disturbed during clearing, construction, operation and post-closure of the mine including, but not limited to, roads, waste dumps, pits and plant site such that site-specific water quality objectives are met at designated monitoring locations.
Minimize erosion of soils by diverting uncontaminated runoff water away from disturbed areas, or other sources of contamination, to meet water quality objectives.

Collect contaminated runoff from construction areas and defined road surfaces, directing this runoff to sedimentation ponds, and treating this runoff with settling aids, if necessary, to meet a minimum effluent discharge limit in diversion or contaminated runoff of 50 mg/L at compliance points, as well as controlling release so as to meet water quality objectives (any deviation from this strategy will be presented in the final sediment control plan to MELP's satisfaction).
Locate sedimentation ponds as close to the sediment source as possible so as to maximize the effectiveness of sediment removal, and minimize contamination of downstream runoff sources.

Use only settling aids shown to be non-toxic to adults, juveniles and eggs of a representative fish species, such as rainbow trout, and to representative aquatic invertebrate species, such as Daphnia spp. or Chironomus spp., and approved by MELP and DFO.

Implement sediment control measures according to approved plans prior to the start of clearing, construction or associated disturbance of all mine structures, including roads, open pits, runoff diversion ditches, tailings lines, waste rock dumps and overburden storage areas and plant site (any deviation from this strategy will be presented in the final sediment control plan to MELP's satisfaction).
The tailings impoundment, main sediment pond and all structures related to controlling and treating sediment generated at the Willow Creek road be engineered structures.

During construction minimize the surface area of un-reclaimed land disturbance by planning construction activities so as to enable surface stabilization and reclamation. This applies particularly to construction of the Willow Creek road.

Cease construction activities or other activities contributing to sediment release, and improve sediment control measures so that the water quality objectives are met whenever sediment release from any disturbed area, or from any sediment control works, causes water quality objectives to be exceeded at a designated monitoring location. Construction activities shall not re-commence until such time as the effectiveness of sediment control measures has been demonstrated through water quality monitoring at the designated locations.

For the construction period, recruitment of qualified independent environmental monitor(s), paid for by the proponent. The monitor shall adhere to a monitoring program agreed to by the review agencies. The monitor shall report to government agencies, but may serve the proponent in their need for internal services. The monitor shall also liaise with the local Environmental Monitoring and Liaison Committee.
Meet water quality objectives at the outlet of the backwater located east of the plant site and south of the BC Rail.
Monitor supernatant quality in the tailings pond, and collect and treat if the sampling in the receiving environment indicates that this is necessary.

If necessary, after further engineering assessment and approval by MELP, include seepage collection ditches in the design of the tailings impoundment and ensure that sufficient area is reserved for their construction.

If necessary, after further engineering assessment and approval by MELP, installation of seepage collection ditches, if tailings supernatant is determined to be of unacceptable quality for release by MELP.

Submit a soil survey, and a soil salvage, handling and storage plan as described in Appendix I of the Application Requirements for a Mine Act Permit Approving the Mine Plan and Reclamation Program: MEI 1998.

Submit, prior to clearing, construction and surface disturbance, an acceptable construction phase environmental monitoring, reporting and response program to minimize environmental impact and control sediment for the construction phase of the main haul road, pre-stripping of mine and wash plant areas using PVC environmental staff and independent environmental monitor.

Submit, prior to clearing, construction or surface disturbance, on an area by area basis, construction plans designed to minimize erosion and soil loss, and avoid, where possible, unstable and readily-erodible soils in the alignment of roads and other structures.

Submit, prior to clearing, construction or surface disturbance, on an area by area basis, a water management/sediment control plan showing all runoff diversion, runoff collection, treatment and discharge structures, and indicating how the works will achieve the sediment control objectives.

Submit, prior to clearing, construction or surface disturbance, an acceptable construction and operational phase surface water, groundwater, sediment quality (using acceptable levels of detection), and aquatic life (including periphyton) monitoring program.

Submit, prior to clearing, construction or surface disturbance, an acceptable background and monitoring program for fish tissue and liver metal levels using sentinel species consistent with that proposed by NDM in the December 2, 1997 report.
Prepare additional characterization of coarse rejects, including sulphur speciation and ICP total elemental analysis.
Prepare, if required, characterization of tailings, including ABA, sulphur speciation and ICP total elemental analysis.

Additional information required by Pine Valley Coal Ltd. prior to initiation of construction and mining are: Acceptable program to characterize ARD/ML construction materials for roadwork and tailings embankments; Development of an acceptable monitoring program for the operational characterization of materials; and If potentially acid generating materials are encountered, an effective ARD/ML prediction and prevention program will be implemented.
Submit, prior to clearing, construction or surface disturbance, analysis of additional samples for particle size distribution and settleability from representative areas, if necessary.
Provide water balance estimates for tailings impoundment including input from precipitation and run off, ground water inputs, and losses due to evaporation and exfiltration.
Implement a no fishing policy, acceptable to DFO and MELP, that prohibits mine construction and operation staff from fishing in Willow Creek.

Before the start of clearing or construction of the north haul road, north sediment pond and any other works that may impact on the backwater area north of the Phase 1 and 2 Dumps, establish, based on existing project material, a summary of fish resources in the identified and impacted backwater area, and assess the loss of associated fish habitat.

Implement a no hunting/firearms policy for the mine, plant site and infrastructure satisfactory to the Regional Manager, Fish and Wildlife, MELP and District Inspector, MEM in consultation with First Nations.
Develop a wildlife-human interaction program to minimize impact to ungulates and bears satisfactory to the Regional Manager, Fish and Wildlife, MELP in consultation with First Nations.
Establish an overview of cumulative effects by the project on resources traditionally utilized by First Nations within the project area.
Establish an employment opportunity plan to identified First Nations, with descriptions of hiring and training policies.
Participate, on request, in any annual review of First Nations' concerns on traditional use, the environment and employment.

Implement, to the satisfaction of the Ministry of Small Business, Tourism and Culture - Archaeology Branch, a "post-harvesting" assessment and mitigation plan for project areas with identified archaeological potential which had poor visibility during the archaeological fieldwork completed by FMA in December, 1997. This work, at the higher elevations of the mine area, is to follow after the initial and more minor ground disturbing aspects of the development have taken place (such as harvesting), but before the soil is stripped or otherwise moved at these locations.
Obtain all necessary Heritage Conservation Act permits to complete the above-noted archaeological work.

Present a plan to MEM and MOH describing the facilities and personal services that will be available to workers. Additionally, there should be an estimate of the total daily volume of effluent discharge from toilets, showers, eating area, laundry (if applicable), etc. This information will indicate the agency with jurisdictional responsibilities for permitting.
Provide a Traffic Impact Study to MOTH to address potential safety issues associated with traffic patterns on access roads.

Provide to MOTH all design details, if required, for a "controlled access highway" as per Section 57 of the Highway Act. Additional conditions may be included on the access permit under the Highway (Industrial) Act.

A qualified engineer or geoscientist would supervise a site monitor. This would involve periodic visits, typically on a weekly schedule (weather dependent) to review construction progress and the effectiveness of the implemented sediment control measures. Any additional control measures which should be implemented for a given section of the road would be identified, and a design memorandum would be prepared while on site.

A site monitor would be present at the site on a full-time basis. He/she would be responsible for: monitoring weather conditions and determining when construction activities should be shut down in areas which are underlain by erodible native soils or fills; directing the implementation of sedimentation control measures identified in the road design and during weekly supervisor visits; monitoring of water quality in receiving waters; and communicating directly with senior management on environmental matters. The site monitor would prepare daily reports and a weekly summary to document construction activities, weather conditions, water quality monitoring data and any water quality concerns, maintain an on-site photographic record, and be responsible for training of construction personnel.

It is recommended that the mine's contingency plan meet Emergency Planning for Industry (CAN/CSA-Z731-M91) in conjunction with the BC Environment Guidelines for Industry Emergency Response Contingency Plans as a minimum. Also, it should be clearly stated that spills that may impact fish-bearing waters be reported to Environment Canada Emergencies at (604) 666-6100.

Provide, prior to construction and surface disturbance, a dust mitigation plan acceptable to MEM and MELP. This plan should include measures to effectively minimize and control dust to the extent practical from tailings, mine roads, coal piles, waste dumps and to ensure that MELP Ambient Air Guidelines are met. Further consideration should also be given to modifications to the material storage and handling plans associated with raw and clean coal and tailings, such as minimizing coal storage and handling at the plant site. In the event that Ambient Air Guidelines are approached at designated monitoring locations off the mine site, an evaluation and assessment of cause and mitigation may be required by MELP.

To produce, to the satisfaction of MELP, an Ambient Air Quality Monitoring and Impact Assessment Plan: to control the emission of fine and coarse particles from project construction and operations to meet the 24 hour Level B fine particulate (PM10) ambient air quality objective of 50 ug/m3 and the level A objective of 1.75 mg/dm2 for the total (coarse and fine) dustfall at designated monitoring locations off the mine site; to install and operate one continuous PM10 monitor and one wind speed and direction monitor at designated monitoring locations off the mine site, at a minimum. The proponent shall have continuous access to the data from these monitors, and shall further reduce particulate emissions if ambient PM10 levels exceed the air quality objective at the monitoring location. Following three years of mine operation, the monitoring program will be reviewed; to install dustfall monitoring equipment at designated monitoring locations off the mine site, and if the ambient air quality objective is not met, shall take further actions to reduce emissions.

Negotiate and conclude, with DFO, in consultation with First Nations, MELP and MEM, an appropriate compensation package for any loss of fish habitat prior to the start of works described in condition 2 above.
Adhere to a progressive reclamation plan to minimize the time between initial disturbance and reclamation in order to reduce the visual quality impact.

Establish a groundwater monitoring and testing program to address potential changes to the water supply and quality for Willow Flats residents. Parameters that should be measured would be indicated by the nature of the chemicals used for the mining operations (fuel, dust suppressants) and leachates (heavy metals, etc.). Frequency of tests shall be adjusted according to results of measurements. If contamination occurs due to mining activities, the proponent must introduce mitigation measures acceptable to MELP, MEM and MOH.
Prior to surface disturbance, provide a soil survey and identification of sensitive sites (with reference to bioterrain map units), and soil storage and handling plan by qualified personnel.

Implement a no hunting/firearms policy for the mine, plant site and infrastructure satisfactory to the Regional Manager, Fish and Wildlife, MELP and District Inspector, MEI in consultation with First Nations.
Develop a wildlife management plan satisfactory to the Regional Manager, Fish and Wildlife, MELP in consultation with First Nations.
Submit an access permit application to MOTH, Dawson Creek, to establish dual tenure with MOF, who currently possess this permit on the proposed access road to the mine.

For the fuel storage facilities, PVC must: Adhere to the CCME Environmental Codes of Practice for fuel tank storage, which encompass and exceed NFC and BCFC requirements; Adopt a written fuel management plan which includes an auditing program; and Design storm water treatment from fueling areas (i.e. the oil-water separator system) in accordance with good engineering principles.

The proponent shall develop and implement a follow-up and monitoring program based on commitments and recommendations contained in the Project Committee Report to ensure that appropriate mitigation and environmental protection strategies are followed and assessed as the project proceeds.

The proponent shall assist in the organization of a local Environmental Monitoring and Liaison Committee, and meet on an agreed basis to keep the Committee members and the general public appraised on the project development.
Before the start of mine operation, the proponent shall complete negotiations and appropriately compensate the affected trapper using the BC Hydro model.
The proponent shall post security under the Mines Act, sufficient to cover all outstanding liabilities through the construction phase of the project.
The proponent shall discuss with the District of Chetwynd potential future mitigation measures if it should be established that the project is negatively impacting the District water supply.

Prior to commencement of construction of the Project, PVC must, to the reasonable satisfaction of the Executive Director: a) develop and implement a follow-up and monitoring program based on commitments and recommendations contained in the Committee Report, to ensure that appropriate mitigation and environmental protection strategies are followed and assessed as the Project proceeds; b) assist in the organization of a local Environmental Monitoring and Liaison Committee, and meet on an agreed basis to keep the Committee members and the general public appraised on the Project development; c) before the start of mine operation, complete negotiations and appropriately compensate the affected trapper, using the BC Hydro model; d) post security under the Mines Act, sufficient to cover all outstanding liabilities through the construction phase of the Project; and e) discuss with the District of Chetwynd potential future mitigation measures if it should be established that the Project is negatively impacting the District water supply.
